newsitem.title: PERU: "Kamikaze" photographer stirs up hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: "Kamikaze" photographer stirs up hostage crisis.

text.p: Photographer Koji Harada found himself at the centre of international controversy on Wednesday after his dash into the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima handed Marxist rebels an unexpected publicity coup.

Harada, a Japanese national now dubbed "the Kamikaze" by the Peruvian press, charged headlong into the diplomatic compound on Tuesday holding up a placard with the name of his employer -- the Kyodo News Agency.

Opinions were divided as to whether his action was evidence of bravery or recklessness, with most colleagues lionising him but government officials from Peru and Japan saying he had endangered himself and others.

More than 15 journalists, part of a group allowed through police lines to photograph the outside of the property, quickly followed Harada's example and were invited into the residence where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas held dozens of VIP hostages.
It was the first time journalists had entered the building since the rebels stormed a lavish cocktail party there on Dec. 17, taking hundreds of guests hostage.

The rebels, dressed in combat gear and carrying automatic rifles, seized the opportunity to hold an impromptu news conference haranguing Peru's President Alberto Fujimori and reiterating demands that the government pardon about 400 jailed comrades.
Dramatic images of the rebels, their faces hidden by red and white neckerchiefs bearing the group's emblem, were broadcast worldwide within minutes.
Fujimori, who had tried to suppress media contact with the rebels by cutting off electricity and telephone lines to the captured residence, was apparently furious with Harada and his colleagues.
"He's annoyed and wouldn't you be? They (the rebels) took the initiative and made a mockery of him," a Government Palace source told Reuters.
Diplomats and Red Cross officials in Lima expressed concern on Wednesday that the unexpected publicity boost for the rebels had set back negotiations to end the crisis by days.
Japanese officials monitoring the crisis in Lima laid the blame for Tuesday's events squarely at the door of Harada and his agency.

Calling Harada's actions "deplorable," the Japanese task force said in a statement that his surprise burst into the residence "could affect the security of the remaining hostages and the attainment of a peaceful resolution."
But Kyodo officials in Lima defended Harada, who they said had risked his life to bring the first images of the rebels to the world.
"The cameraman was scared at the time, and was putting his life in danger," a Kyodo News Agency official told Reuters.
The official said Kyodo had been granted access to the residence after arranging an interview with the rebels. He declined to say how the interview had been arranged.
Earlier on Tuesday a notice held up to one of the windows of the residence had said that Kyodo could enter the residence.
Few fellow journalists blamed Harada for what they saw as his daring action in quest of the story, however -- even those who did not manage to get into the besieged compound.
"It was a question of nerve," one sound technician for a foreign television agency said. "He went for it, then the others did. Our guy didn't."
